analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate lowest drug prices and lets seniors import prescriptions from Canada.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, never left House committees and died at the end of the 109th Congress without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate the lowest possible prices for prescription drugs covered by the new Medicare drug benefit, similar to how the Veterans Affairs and Defense Departments buy drugs in bulk, and to publicly disclose those prices. It also would have struck the Medicare law's 'noninterference' clause, which bars the government from negotiating drug prices. Separately, it would have required the FDA to create a waiver letting Medicare beneficiaries personally import up to a 90-day supply of FDA-approved prescription drugs from licensed Canadian pharmacies.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries would gain if the bill passed: the government would negotiate and publish the lowest possible prices for covered drugs, and seniors could legally buy FDA-approved prescriptions from licensed Canadian pharmacies, where identical drugs often sell for less. Taxpayers would also benefit from lower program costs.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate the best possible prices for Medicare-covered drugs, using authority similar to that exercised by the Veterans Affairs and Defense Departments when buying drugs in bulk, and to widely disclose the negotiated prices.
Strikes the 'noninterference' provision in the Medicare law that currently prohibits the government from interfering in drug price negotiations between manufacturers and plans.

Requires the FDA to issue a waiver allowing Medicare beneficiaries to personally import FDA-approved, non-controlled prescription drugs from licensed Canadian pharmacies, limited to a 90-day supply with a valid U.S. prescription, not for resale.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the cost: negotiated 'best price' rules and legal personal importation from Canada would compress the prices they can charge in the U.S. market, the world's largest prescription drug market.

drawbacks.text: Broad price negotiation could reduce drug manufacturers' revenues, which the industry argues would mean less investment in developing new medicines.

Personal drug importation carries safety oversight challenges even with safeguards; the bill addresses this by limiting imports to FDA-approved drugs from registered, licensed Canadian pharmacies with a 90-day supply cap, but regulators would still bear the burden of enforcing those conditions.
Requiring disclosure of negotiated prices could reveal pricing strategies to manufacturers' competitors and complicate negotiations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors paying U.S. retail prices that in many cases are multiples of Canadian prices, the potential savings are substantial, and the bill includes concrete safety conditions on importation. The main trade-off is the industry's argument that lower negotiated prices would reduce incentives for new drug development — a real cost, though the federal government already negotiates bulk prices for VA and DoD purchases without abandoning drug procurement.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees and their health subcommittees for the rest of the two-year Congress and was never taken up, so it died without any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Stephen Lynch introduced the Prescription Drug Affordability Act of 2005 in the House on February 2, 2005.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and within two weeks both referred it to their health subcommittees.
No further action was taken for the remainder of the 109th Congress, and the bill had no cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers were better off: the Medicare law's ban on government price negotiation and the prohibition on importing cheaper drugs from Canada both remained in place, so drug companies kept the U.S. market as their highest-price market and the new Medicare drug benefit launched without government price negotiation. Seniors continued paying the prevailing U.S. prices.

for.name: Rep. Stephen F. Lynch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require Medicare drug price negotiation and permit personal importation of prescriptions from Canada.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 2, 2005, sent it to the Health Subcommittee, and never took further action; the bill died there.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 2, 2005, sent it to the Health Subcommittee, and never took further action.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan split appears in the record; the only named supporter was a Democrat, and the Republican-controlled committees took no action.

industries.note: The bill would have required the government to negotiate and disclose the lowest prices for Medicare-covered drugs, replacing the 'noninterference' clause that keeps the government out of price talks, and would have legalized personal importation of cheaper Canadian drugs. Its death left the industry's pricing structure and the ban on importation intact.

Legal personal importation would have given Medicare beneficiaries a channel to buy some prescriptions from Canadian pharmacies instead of domestic ones, shifting some sales abroad. The effect was limited to a 90-day personal-use supply and never took effect.
